notation.typical: US imports from China ≈ 0.002 (1987) to ≈ 0.047 (2007) overall

notation.meaning: End year of the exposure period

blocks.md: **Following individual workers by the industry they worked in in 1991 — so that later moves do not select the sample — those in industries hit harder by Chinese imports had lower cumulative earnings over 1992–2007, spent more time switching employers and in nonemployment, and drew more disability benefits. The losses fall on low- and middle-wage workers; high-wage workers move and recover.**

- **Exposure**: $\Delta IP_{j}$ = change in US imports from China 1991–$\tau$ over 1991 absorption in the worker's 1991 industry ([Import Penetration](note:import-penetration)).
- **Instrument**: the same using other high-income countries' imports from China, with absorption lagged three years ([Shift-Share Instrument](note:shift-share-instrument)).
- **Outcome**: cumulative earnings 1992–$\tau$, in multiples (× 100) of average annual earnings in 1988–91.
- **Sample**: 1% random sample of US workers from the Social Security Administration's Master Earnings File, born 1943–1970, with high labor-force attachment in 1988–91 (earnings ≥ 1,600 hours at the real 1989 federal minimum wage each year). Standard errors clustered by 3-digit industry.

blocks.md: OLS: −2.939 (1.150) without controls to −6.099 (1.395) with controls. 2SLS: −6.883 (1.351) to **−6.864 (2.477)** in the full specification (column 9). N = 508,129.

**Magnitude**: ΔIP is 7.30 pp at the 75th and 0.62 pp at the 25th percentile, so the implied difference in cumulative earnings is $-6.86 \times (7.30 - 0.62) \approx -46\%$ of initial annual earnings.

| Top | −0.22 (2.07) | −9.15~ | +6.69 |
High-wage workers leave exposed employers and make up the losses elsewhere; low-wage workers lose at their initial firm and after moving.

- **Why track workers by initial industry**: people still in a region or industry later are a selected sample; fixing the 1991 "location" avoids that selection.
- **Inequality**: impacts are strong outside the top of the distribution.
